blogTitle: Color Matching Guide for Wall Art - How to Choose Perfect Colours?
videoTitle: How do you choose wall art colours that actually work in your home?
script:
How do you choose wall art colours that actually work in your home?

Choosing wall art colours can feel overwhelming — but it really doesn't have to be.

Should art match your walls, contrast with them, or pull from your accent colours?

The truth is there's no single right answer — but there are proven strategies that make it much easier.

My favourite place to start is the colour wheel — it makes colour relationships suddenly make sense.

Primary colours mix to make secondary colours, which mix again to make tertiaries — that's the whole foundation.

Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the wheel — they create bold, high-energy contrast.

Analogous colours sit next to each other on the wheel — they feel calm, cohesive and really easy to live with.

Understanding these basic relationships gives you real confidence when choosing art colours.

One of the simplest strategies: pull a colour from your existing furnishings and find art that echoes it.

A little tip I love: hold a colour swatch from a print next to your cushions, rug or sofa before you buy.

These Japanese sunset prints are a beautiful example of high contrast — bold black and white that works with almost any palette.

If your room is mostly neutral, art with one strong accent colour can do a lot of the heavy lifting.

These abstract framed prints are a great example — just enough colour to anchor a neutral space without overwhelming it.

Take care not to choose art purely because it matches — sometimes a slight contrast is what makes it interesting.

Warm colours — terracotta, rust, ochre — make a room feel cosy and grounded.

These Moroccan-inspired prints bring in that warm earthy palette beautifully — terracotta, deep red and gold all at once.

Cool colours — soft blues, greens, greys — create a feeling of calm and space in a room.

If you're unsure which palette suits your home, look at what you're naturally drawn to in your textiles and furniture first.

These three art prints use a muted, earthy tonal palette — a brilliant option if you want cohesion without drama.

A very common mistake: choosing art that blends so well it disappears. A little contrast always helps it read.

The 60-30-10 rule is a handy guide: 60% dominant colour, 30% secondary, 10% accent — art often fills that accent role.

These prints work brilliantly in that accent role — a considered pop of colour in an otherwise neutral scheme.

If you're forgetful like me, take a photo of your room before you go shopping — the real colours are always different to what you remember.

Tonal art — using light and dark shades of the same colour — is one of the most forgiving approaches for beginners.

These modern living room prints use a restrained tonal palette — clean, simple, and endlessly versatile.

Dark walls are having a real moment — and art actually stands out beautifully against them.

Take care with very busy patterned art in a room that already has lots of pattern — it can quickly feel chaotic.

A practical tip: use the paint colour on the back of a frame or mount card to test how it reads on your wall before committing.

Whether you go bold or subtle, the key is simply understanding how colours relate to each other.

Once you know the basics, choosing wall art colours stops feeling like guesswork and starts feeling enjoyable.

Did you know styling your home doesn't have to be guesswork?

We've built a free set of Home Decor tools and styling guides…

From colour theory and design principles to gallery wall layouts and art sizing. Download them all from our site!

Find all you need to transform your home into a calming oasis!

Happy Decorating!
